name: Product page copy and layout (PDP)
asked_as: our product page does not convert
product page copy for the new launch
too many returns for wrong size
make our product page look like this one
people visit but don't add to cart
outcome: One product page, written in full and laid out for a phone, that answers the doubts stopping this product's buyers (found in reviews, returns and chats) with real proof beside the buy button, states fit and limits as numbers, frames the price honestly, shows what Indian consumer rules require, and comes with one number to watch, a guardrail and a fallback line.
first_principles: A product page is a decision, not a description. Its job is to remove the two or three doubts that stop this product's buyers, in the order they have them. Those doubts are in returns, 3-star reviews, pre-purchase chats and 'what almost stopped you' answers, not in the founder's feature list.

The first phone screen does most of the work: rating, the promise, price, variant, the button and one risk line under it. Most visitors never scroll past it, and more shoppers swipe the whole gallery than read the whole page, so the gallery is a second sales page, not a set of angles.

Returns are a page problem. A wrong expectation (runs small, darker than it looks, holds less) is answered with a number where the buyer decides, plus a pointer to the product that fits them. Stopping the wrong-fit order protects more profit than one more sale.

Proof answers one objection at a time: a real review from a different kind of buyer per doubt, placed by the decision, beats a wall of stars. Under about 80 reviews, collecting more can matter more than the copy.
Match the traffic. An ad that sells one benefit to one buyer needs the page to open on that same promise; a page that lists every benefit converts worse for each ad that sends people to it.

Price is framed, never faked: cost per use, what is in the box, the bundle saving in rupees, a strike-through only against a price it really sold at. In India these are legal duties as well as good selling: the full price up front, no false urgency, no charges sprung at checkout.

questions.ask: Which product page should I work on first?
questions.why: The page with the most lost profit pays back first; a page for a product that loses money should not be improved at all.

options.label: The one you named
options.con: may not be where most profit leaks

options.label: The one losing the most gross profit
options.con: may not be the one you had in mind

questions.default: The page with the most lost gross profit: high sessions, add-to-cart rate well below the store's average, positive gross profit per order
questions.settle_with_data: Rank product pages by sessions times the gap between their add-to-cart rate and the store's average, weighted by gross profit per order, over 30 to 90 days (Shopify or GA4). Say the ranking and its source in one line.

questions.ask: Who mostly lands on this page: people from one ad, search shoppers, or a mix?
questions.why: Ad visitors need the ad's promise on the first screen; search and returning visitors need specs, comparison and proof sooner.

options.label: People from one ad angle
options.pro: the page can open on exactly what they were promised
options.con: other visitors are served a little less

options.label: Search and returning shoppers
options.pro: lead with specs, fit and comparison
options.con: cold ad visitors may not get the why

options.label: A mix
options.con: the promise must be broad enough to hold; angle pages can follow

questions.default: A mix, with the top ad's winning promise in the headline
skip_if: the brief says where traffic comes from
questions.settle_with_data: Read sessions to this page by source and campaign (GA4 or Shopify) and the top ads sending traffic with their headlines. If one paid angle sends most sessions, lead with it.

questions.ask: Copy only, or copy and layout (section order, gallery, buy box)?
questions.why: If the layout hides the proof or the price, new copy alone cannot fix the page.

options.label: Copy only
options.con: the layout's leaks stay

options.label: Copy plus a layout plan and gallery shot list
options.pro: fixes order and proof placement; your team or theme editor builds it
options.con: a little theme work

options.label: Copy plus a built theme section
options.pro: ready to switch on in the theme editor
options.con: needs theme access on a duplicate theme and your yes to publish

questions.default: Copy plus a layout plan and gallery shot list
skip_if: the brief limits the job to copy
questions.settle_with_data: Render the live page at phone width: if the rating, price, button and a risk line are not all on the first screen, or reviews and guarantee sit far below, the layout is part of the job.

questions.ask: Do you sell in India only, or abroad too?
questions.why: It decides the legal disclosures, the price and tax lines, COD and delivery wording.

options.label: India only
options.pro: one set of rules and one currency
options.con: none

options.label: India and abroad
options.con: disclosures and delivery lines per market

skip_if: the store has a single currency and ships to India only
questions.settle_with_data: Check the store's markets, currencies and shipping zones.

data_map.question: Is the page the leak?
data_map.data: Product views, add-to-cart rate against the store's average, checkout and orders, by device and source
data_map.if_missing: a phone walk-through; the gain is marked unmeasured

data_map.question: What doubts stop buyers?
data_map.data: Review themes with counts and exact quotes, 3-star reviews first; repeated pre-purchase questions

data_map.question: What comes back, and why?
data_map.data: Return and exchange reasons per 100 orders, by variant; exchanges by size from and to
data_map.if_missing: review complaints as a stand-in, labelled

data_map.question: What were visitors promised before they landed?
data_map.data: Sessions by source and campaign; the top ads' headlines and hooks

data_map.question: How far do people get on the page?
data_map.data: Scroll depth, gallery swipes, taps on the size chart and reviews
data_map.if_missing: assume most never leave the first screen and the gallery

data_map.data: Chats that mention price; rival prices for the same product delivered
data_map.if_missing: frame the price with per-use cost and what is in the box

look_for: Where it leaks: healthy views with add-to-cart well below the store's average is the page; add-to-cart fine but few orders is cart or checkout, where page copy will not help; few views is traffic or collection placement.

The first phone screen at 390 px: are the rating, the promise, the price, the variant picker, the button and a risk line all visible without scrolling? A headline that is only the product name wastes the most-read line.
3-star reviews: they name the real doubt in the buyer's words ('lovely but runs small', 'smaller than it looks in photos').
Returns by variant: one size or colour with far more returns than its share of orders means the page sets a wrong expectation for it.
One-way exchanges: most exchanges going from M to L means the chart runs small. Say so on the page with the measurement, not 'true to size'.
Repeated pre-purchase questions (delivery to my pincode, COD, real silver or plated, washable, will it fit my space): each one is a missing line near the button.
Ad-to-page mismatch: the top ad promises one benefit and the page opens on another.
Proof far from the decision: reviews at the bottom, the guarantee folded inside an accordion, no photo reviews, press logos with no quote.
Price with no frame: no per-use cost, bundle saving in percent rather than rupees, a strike-through price with no real sales history behind it.
A gallery that does not sell: one angle, no in-hand or on-body shot for scale, no 'what is in the box', no image that answers the top doubt.
India legal gaps: MRP inclusive of taxes, net quantity, country of origin, maker or importer details, seller details and a grievance contact missing; a COD or shipping fee shown only at checkout.
Machine copy: lines that would fit any rival's product.

hypothesis_patterns.evidence: one return reason above about 10% of this product's returns, or a variant whose returns far exceed its share of orders
hypothesis_patterns.bet: state the limit as a number at each decision point, add a scale image to the gallery and a 'not for you if' link to the better-fit product

hypothesis_patterns.evidence: a question in about 10% or more of pre-purchase chats
hypothesis_patterns.bet: answer it in the line under the button and in the first FAQ

hypothesis_patterns.pattern: Proof sits far from the decision
hypothesis_patterns.evidence: reviews exist but below the fold; rating not by the title
hypothesis_patterns.bet: rating above the title and 3 objection-matched reviews beside the buy box

hypothesis_patterns.pattern: The page breaks the ad's promise
hypothesis_patterns.evidence: most sessions come from one ad angle that the first screen does not mention
hypothesis_patterns.bet: headline and subhead in the ad's winning words, or an angle page for that traffic

hypothesis_patterns.evidence: price comes up in chats; rivals look cheaper on the shelf
hypothesis_patterns.bet: per-use cost, what is in the box and the bundle saving in rupees; trust lines above the price and under the button

hypothesis_patterns.pattern: A weak first screen on mobile
hypothesis_patterns.evidence: phone add-to-cart rate well below desktop on the same page
hypothesis_patterns.bet: rebuild the first screen and the gallery order for a phone

decisions.ask: Which promise should lead the page?

options.label: The outcome most buyers name in reviews
options.pro: true for the widest group, in their words
options.con: may not match a specific ad
options.when: traffic is a mix and returns are low

options.label: The top ad's winning angle
options.pro: message match, so ad visitors convert
options.con: other visitors are served a little less
options.when: one paid angle sends most sessions

options.label: The biggest doubt, answered as a promise
options.con: can read defensive if overdone
options.when: returns cost more gross profit than the conversion gap

decisions.recommend: From the data: one paid angle with most sessions, lead with it; returns costing more gross profit than the add-to-cart gap, lead with the answered doubt; otherwise the most-named outcome that the claims sheet can prove.

decisions.ask: Rewrite the live page, test it against the current one, or build a separate page for ad traffic?

options.label: Rewrite the live page
options.con: no clean read of the gain
options.when: under about 30 orders a month, or fixing a clear error (a legal line, a wrong fact)

options.label: Test against the current page
options.con: needs traffic and a few weeks
options.when: enough orders for the test to reach a verdict

options.label: A separate page for one ad angle
options.pro: exact match for that ad's buyers
options.con: one more page to keep up to date
options.when: ads test different buyers or benefits on the same product

decisions.recommend: Legal or factual errors are fixed live at once. Above about 30 orders a month, test the rewrite; below it, rewrite and read in matching weeks. Add an angle page only when one ad angle scales and the main page cannot lead with it.

rules: The first phone screen (390 px wide) holds the rating with its count, the promise in under 10 words, the price, the variant picker, the button and one risk line directly under it.
Every claim traces to the claims sheet; when the proof supports only a narrower line, narrow the claim or let one customer say it in their words.

A limit that changes who should buy is a number ('chest 102 cm on M', 'fits a 15-inch laptop'), stated in a bullet, the details table, the first FAQ and under the button, with a 'not for you if' link to the better-fit product.
Each top doubt gets one real review from a different kind of buyer, placed by the decision, with first name, date and source; counts of reviewers stay in the notes, not the copy.

Price framing uses real numbers only: the bundle saving in rupees, cost per use, what is in the box. A strike-through only against a price it really sold at; from 1 January 2027 a price cut shows the lowest price of the past 30 days.
No false urgency or scarcity: stock and deadlines come from live inventory and real end dates. No pre-ticked add-ons. COD and shipping fees are shown before checkout, not sprung at it.

For India the page shows: MRP inclusive of all taxes, net quantity, country of origin, the maker, packer or importer name and address, the seller's name and address, customer care and grievance contacts, return, refund and exchange terms, delivery estimate, and best-before where it applies; from 1 January 2027 also the GSTIN or MSME number.
Guarantee, return and delivery lines match the live policy pages in substance; a pincode check line sits near the button.
Copy is in the brand's words, at its reading level; Hinglish or a regional-language headline only when the reviews are written that way.
The gallery shows the real product as it ships; no AI-made person, photo or quote is presented as a customer.
Live copy holds no placeholder ([X], TBC, 'link here'); an unknown fact gets the safest true wording or is left out.

checks: Every claim and price line through check-ad-copy-for-policy-and-claims (Indian consumer rules, dark patterns, comparisons).
Walk the rendered page on a phone as the buyer from the top ad: the first screen keeps the ad's promise and the top doubt is answered within a thumb's reach of the button.
senior_review: If I were the buyer who returned this, would this page have stopped me ordering the wrong one?
Which of the top three doubts is still not answered near the button?
Does every number (rating, count, measurement, price, delivery days) come from a dated source?
Would a consumer officer find a missing disclosure, a fake strike-through or a dark pattern?
Does the page still sell if the visitor sees only the first screen and swipes the gallery?
Is there one number to watch, a guardrail, a read date and a fallback line?
